catalog_quote: 5.1.3.2 Druckakzent Tucker/Bryan und Tucker sprechen in allen Arbeiten zum Kalenjin von 'stressed syllables', 'shift in stress' usw.; der Druckakzent scheint aber nach ihren Angaben mit Hochton oder Steigton korreliert zu sein, und markiert werden bei ihnen nur die Tonhöhen. In Heines Sogoo-Vokabular sind Druckakzent und Tonhöhe unabhängig bezeichnet (Heine 1973). Der Druckakzent geht hier mit hohem oder mit fallendem Ton einher, ist aber weiter nicht vorhersagbar. Bei meinen Aufzeichnungen habe ich keine Anzeichen für Druckakzent in phonemischer Funktion feststellen können und bezeichne ihn deshalb nicht. Phonetisch sind betonte Silben erkennbar, und zwar immer in Verbindung mit nicht-tiefem Ton. 5.1.3.3 Ton Tucker (1964: 457) gibt für die Kalenjin-Sprachen drei einfache Töne (Hoch, Mittel, Tief) an; hinzu kommen Gleittöne, nämlich ein fallender Ton und drei positionsbedingte Steigtöne (Hoch-Tief, Hoch-Mittel, Mittel-Hoch).

new_statements.translation: Stress accent. Tucker/Bryan and Tucker speak in all their works on Kalenjin of 'stressed syllables', 'shift in stress' etc.; according to their data, however, the stress accent seems to be correlated with high tone or rising tone, and they mark only the pitches. In Heine's Sogoo [Okiek] vocabulary, stress accent and pitch are marked independently (Heine 1973). Here the stress accent goes together with high or with falling tone, but is otherwise not predictable. In my own recordings I could find no indication of stress accent in a phonemic function and therefore do not mark it. Phonetically, stressed syllables are recognisable, and always in combination with non-low tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Okiek, like the rest of Kalenjin, is a tone language (Rottland: high/mid/low plus contour tones for Kalenjin; Micheli 2018: H, M, L in Mariashoni Okiek; Ochieng 2025: H vs L with grammatical case/aspect tone in Nessuit Okiek). Word stress is not contrastive and has no fixed position: perceptual prominence sits on a syllable carrying non-low (high or falling) tone, and in the one Okiek source that marks it independently (Heine's 1973 Sogoo list) its location is 'otherwise not predictable'. No positional stress rule is stated by any source; the two modern Okiek grammars describe tone only and never mention stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Rottland only notes that earlier authors' (Tucker & Bryan) 'stress' marks coincide with high/rising tone, and that in Sogoo stress may fall on a high- or a falling-toned syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (elicited words/short phrases: Heine's Sogoo vocabulary items, Rottland's field recordings). Rottland's own-recordings sentence is a statement about Kalenjin as a whole, whose corpus includes Kinare Okiek and Sogoo Okiek (and Akie); the Sogoo-specific sentence is his report of Heine 1973's transcription. Micheli 2018 (p.5, p.10) explicitly leaves suprasegmentals in connected speech unanalysed.
new_statements.identity_note: Rottland's first-hand sentence ('no phonemic stress; stressed syllables always with non-low tone') is made for Kalenjin as a whole in a chapter whose corpus includes two Okiek varieties — Kinare Okiek (extinct remnant, central Kenya) and Sogoo Okiek (= Glottolog dialect sogo1244 under okie1245, Kipchorng'wonek group, SW Mau) — plus Akie of Tanzania (Glottolog treats Akie as a separate language mosi1247 [mwy]); the Sogoo-specific sentence is second-hand from Heine 1973. The two modern open grammars are of Nuclear Okiek (nucl1432): Micheli 2018 = Mariashoni/Morisionig, Ochieng 2025 = Nessuit/Tiepkwererek (Eastern Mau, Nakuru County); both describe tone only. König, Heine & Legère 2015 ('stress, or pitch accent, clearly exists but does not appear to [be] phonologically distinctive', p.25) describes Akie (mosi1247), a sister language, and should not be filed under okie1245 except as corroboration.

new_statements.quote: rendering of Okiek here is simplified in one important way: I do not indicate tonal distinctions, which carry both semantic meaning and grammatical information. This impoverishes the detail and accuracy of the transcription, but tonal distinctions are not central to the analyses presented here. Okiek has a series of four unvoiced stop phonemes that become voiced after nasals, and after /l/: /p/, /t/, /c/, and /k/.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Okiek is described as having tonal distinctions that carry both lexical (semantic) and grammatical information; the author leaves tone unmarked in her transcriptions. Nothing is said about word stress or accent placement.
new_statements.identity_note: Kratz 1994 describes Kipchornwonek and Kaplelach Okiek of Narok District (bases near Sogoo/Olkerei and Entasekera), the variety she calls most similar to Kipsigis. Tucker 1964 is about Nandi, Kipsigis, Keyo, Tugen and Päkot (Pokot), not Okiek; no Okiek/Dorobo material found in it. Rottland 1982's existing statement is a Kalenjin-wide remark with Sogoo (Okiek) vocabulary evidence from Heine 1973.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3 'Tones' p.10: 'Ogiek seems to recognize at least three different tones: H, M, L. Modulated tones appear as a consequence of the contact of two different kind of tones on two distinct syllables' and tone analysis admittedly incomplete (p.5: 'Due to the scarcity of good materials for the analysis of suprasegmental phenomena.. these parts need surely further investigation'). No statement about word stress/accent anywhere (the word 'stressed' is used only for geminate consonants and pragmatic emphasis).
